author: Press Association
description:
• Chair David Kogan insists regulator has power to act

  • City have appealed against Premier League’s charges

The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will have “absolute power” to force Manchester City’s owners to sell if they are ultimately found to have run the club improperly, the watchdog’s chair has said.

Manchester City have been found guilty of circumventing Premier League rules by an independent commission, which found they set up “sham” commercial arrangements to inflate revenues or reduce costs by over £900m over a nine-season period.

Continue reading...
title: Football regulator has ‘absolute power’ to force Manchester City sale if verdict upheld

author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
description:
A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors

In South Korea, they call them jagyeongdan, a word that sits somewhere between a vigilante group and a neighbourhood watch.

Each night they don hi-vis vests, pick up their selfie sticks, and gather around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge: a stranded shark affectionately known as Bukang-i.

Continue reading...
title: After dark, these YouTubers watch over an unlikely charge – a shark stuck in a South Korean canal

author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
description:
Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking

From politicians taking bribes to bullying and harassment in City firms, leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel.

Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking.

Continue reading...
title: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others

author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
description:
UK study of 6,000 patients shows shedding 5% of body weight may help cut the risk of stroke and heart disease

Losing just 5% of your body weight in middle age can reduce inflammation, lower the risk of stroke and make your heart as healthy as if you had never gained weight, research suggests.

Millions of men and women worldwide gain weight as they age, putting extra stress on their body, reducing quality of life and doing significant damage to their cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Continue reading...
title: Weight loss in middle age can restore cardiovascular health, research suggests

author: Lucy Mangan
description:
From incontinence to reconstructive bladder surgery, ketamine’s popularity with the young is a public health crisis in motion. But is Dooley the right person to get to grips with it?

Stacey Dooley’s latest documentary, Down the K Hole, lands as part of a new batch of three from the presenter. One explores the death in barracks of 19-year-old Jaysley Beck and asks how well the army protects its female soldiers from sexual assault and harassment; another investigates the phenomenon of women who are killed by falling and how often domestic abuse may have been involved.

Down the K Hole follows the stories of a handful of ketamine addicts in recovery, representatives of what we are told is a 20% increase in UK admissions involving use of the drug since 2023. Dooley spends four months embedded in Acorn Recovery Projects, a rehab centre in Stockport. It is not really made clear what “embedded” means. She appears to turn up in the mornings, rather than live the
title: Stacey Dooley: Down the K Hole review – the weird tale of how you can order ketamine quicker than pizza

author: Agencies
description:
• Detroit erase 22-point deficit to beat Boston 121-113

  • Paul George scores 38 points on Celtics debut in defeat

  • Robinson scores 15 of his 21 points in fourth quarter

Duncan Robinson scored 15 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter as the Detroit Pistons reeled off 23 unanswered points to beat the visiting Boston Celtics 121-113 in the NBA’s regular-season opener on Tuesday afternoon.

Jalen Duren and Cade Cunningham scored 22 points apiece for the Pistons, who led the Eastern Conference with 60 wins last season.

Continue reading...
title: Robinson sparks 23-0 run as Pistons stun Celtics in NBA season opener

author: Chris Stein in Washington
description:
Billionaire ex-mayor of New York City is focusing funds on House races to help Democrats retake majority in midterms

  • US politics live – latest updates

The billionaire Michael Bloomberg will spend $80m to help Democratic candidates in the midterm elections, US media reported on Tuesday, a significant infusion of cash for a party that has recently struggled with fundraising as it seeks to win control of Congress.

The reported donations came as Donald Trump announced on Tuesday he intended to spend a total of $400m to aid Republican candidates, wit
title: Michael Bloomberg spends $80m on Democrats as Trump moves $400m to Republican candidates

author: Barney Ronay at Parc des Princes
description:
Fire, noise, fury, a sense of empty energy. And across town, a football match too.

Do any of these randomly pitched autumnal Champions League fixtures mean anything? Probably not when you’re Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona, and the only game in town is risk-free TV income and a semi-guaranteed place in the knockout stuff.

Continue reading...
title: Doué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSG

author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
description:
Andoni Iraola and Iñigo Pérez parked their long and close friendship in the buildup to the Champions League duel between two old Athletic Bilbao teammates. They will have a humdinger of a contest to dissect when communications are restored. Liverpool, driven by Alexis Mac Allister and ignited by Rio Ngumoha, recovered from two goals down against Villarreal to maintain their 100% record in the competition in emphatic style.

Mac Allister struck twice as Liverpool fought back from a tepid start to record a third successive win in all competitions. They were given a scare when Tani Oluwaseyi volleyed in a late third for Villarreal but were well deserving of their latest impressive result.

Continue reading...
title: Mac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win against Villarreal

author: Will Unwin at the Etihad Stadium
description:
Enzo Maresca has called for Manchester City to make their own noise on the pitch to drown out the cacophony surrounding them but maybe a quiet night at the Etihad Stadium was what they needed all along. AEK Athens were easily dispatched in a businesslike manner, as Phil Foden announced his return to form with a hat-trick to get City’s Champions League campaign back on track after being pummelled by Paris Saint-Germain.

The match was uneven throughout as Foden shone on the wing and later down the middle, with goals from Elliot Anderson and Rayan Cherki helping to ease City to victory in front of half-full stands. Stavros Pilios’s consolation was more a reward for the boisterous fans in yellow and black than for the overall efforts of the visitors.
title: Foden hat-trick helps Manchester City cut through noise and crush AEK Athens

author: Nick Robins-Early
description:
Elon Musk’s company reports a 161% growth in revenue year over year driven by its Starlink and AI segments

SpaceX released its second-ever public earnings report on Tuesday, revealing a far better quarter than Wall Street projected. Elon Musk’s company, which encompasses rockets, artificial intelligence and satellite communications, reported a 161% growth in revenue year over year, driven by its Starlink and AI segments.

The company declared $14.58bn in revenue against analysts’ projected $12.72bn. SpaceX reported earnings per share of 35 cents and a net income of $4.4bn. The company’s stock, which started the day down around 8% for the year, shot up 2% in after hours trading immediately after the results.

Continue reading...
title: SpaceX’s revenue jumps in second-ever earnings report amid Starlink turmoil

author: Richard Adams Education editor
description:
Government expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudice

Schools and colleges in England will be expected to take a tougher stance against antisemitism after a report found that three out of five Jewish students said they had been affected.

Sir David Bell, the former chief inspector of Ofsted who was commissioned by the government to lead the independent review, said he found many cases of antisemitism going unreported or unchallenged by students and teachers.

Continue reading...
title: Schools in England must recognise antisemitism as distinct category of harm, report says

author: Press Association
description:
• Former world No 1 loses 4-2 to Jordan Brown in Belfast

  • ‘I don’t see a future with snooker in it,’ says tearful Allen

Mark Allen said he was in a “bad place” and his snooker career could be over after losing to Jordan Brown in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open in Belfast.

The 40-year-old was playing his first match since his world championship semi-final loss to Wu Yize in April. Allen missed a match-ball black off the spot at 16-15 in front and went on to lose the deciding frame to Wu, who went on to win the title.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I’m in a bad place’: Mark Allen says his snooker career may be over after defeat

author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
description:
Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m

  • UK politics live – latest updates

A senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backers Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party.

James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.

Continue reading...
title: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations

author: Editorial
description:
The government did not throw a ‘protective ring’ around social care, and vulnerable people were left exposed

The families of the 43,000 care home residents in the UK whose deaths between March 2020 and July 2022 were either caused by, or contributed to, by the Covid pandemic, have waited a long time for the official verdict on the way they were treated. The report published on Tuesday confirmed what many have been saying for a long time. In the first, panicked stages of lockdown, residents and their care workers were “something of an afterthought”. The “protective ring” around care homes referred to by Matt Hancock, the former health and care secretary, was a fiction.

These are scathing judgments. What actually happened, starting in March 2020, was that about 30,000 people were discharged from hospital to care homes in ord
title: The Guardian view on Covid-19 and care homes: the inquiry’s scathing verdict must be heeded | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats

Canadians are proving to be a voice of sanity. In roundly rejecting the idea of separating from Canada, voters in the oil- and gas-rich province of Alberta sensibly backed the nation-building strategy of the prime minister, Mark Carney. He has put Alberta at the centre of his plan to make Canada an energy superpower that is “much less dependent on the United States”.

Donald Trump’s trade war and threats
title: The Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald Trump | Editorial

author: Scott Murray
description:
⚽ Updates from the 8pm BST kick-off at Anfield
⚽ Football clockwatch | Live scores | Table | Mail Scott

This is a match between Liverpool and Villarreal. One of the top teams in England versus one of the top teams in Spain. The Premier League versus La Liga. The Redmen versus the Yellow Submarine. And yet it’s really none of that. Some things go down to the micro level, as Sid Lowe explains with trademark eloquence in the first part (there will be more, and you will enjoy it) of your required pre-match reading …

Andoni Iraola versus his close compadre Iñigo Pérez kicks off at 8pm BST. Hasi da! It’s on!

Continue reading...
title: Liverpool v Villarreal: Champions League – live

author: Simon Burnton
description:
⚽ Updates from Tuesday’s Champions League games
⚽ Liverpool v Villarreal | Live scores | Table | Mail Simon

Hello world! Another busy night lies ahead in Europe and in the English Football League, with much attention destined to be focused on Paris, scene in recent days of violence and looting but host tonight of one of the prestige fixtures of the group stage as the teams sitting first and second in the nascent table after two fixtures, five-time champions Barcelona and double reigning champions Paris Saint Germain, meet at the Parc des Princes.

Manchester City, meanwhile, may be without Erling Haaland for the visit of AEK Athens, who are promising not to go all-out defensive for a trip to a side Marko Nikolic, the Greek side’s Serbian coach, described as “one of the best
title: PSG v Barcelona, Manchester City v AEK Athens, and more: Champions League – live

author: Presented by Annie Kelly with Tom McIlroy ; producer Angus Neale ; senior producer Leonore Schick ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
description:
A man has been charged after the Australian MP Helen Haines was allegedly attacked with a car outside her electorate office in the state of Victoria.

Haines, who is an independent MP, has lost one leg as a result of the incident and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg. Police say 43-year-old Brendan Nugent has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and causing harm to a commonwealth public official.

Annie Kelly speaks to Guardian Australia political editor Tom McIlroy

Continue reading...
title: Australian MP Helen Haines attacked with car: what we know so far - The Latest

author: Ben Quinn
description:
Jurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’

Tommy Robinson told the Daily Mail’s editor he would make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”, the harassment trial of the far-right activist has been told.

The threat was made in a voicemail message left on the phone of Ted Verity as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, allegedly waged a campaign of harassment against journalists from the newspaper.

Continue reading...
title: Tommy Robinson threatened to make families of Mail journalists ‘famous’, court hears

author: Jeremy Whittle
description:
Redundancies beckon as British Cycling restructures while former cyclists and employees raise concerns over return of ‘toxic culture’

British Cycling’s most successful world track championships campaign in over a decade, in which they topped the medal table in the first qualifying event for the 2028 Olympic Games, was achieved against a backdrop of allegations of misconduct and looming redundancies.

Despite a traumatic buildup to the championships in Shanghai, which saw star sprinter Matt Richardson withdrawn from competition on the eve of the event due to allegations of “discriminatory remarks,” the British squad recovered to win six gold medals, three silver and three bronze medals.

Continue reading...
title: British Cycling’s best world championships since 2012 overshadowed by off-track issues

author: Ella Baron
description: Continue reading...
title: Ella Baron on the aftermath of the riots in France – cartoon

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Damien Conrad makes the case for local food hubs, Simon Tompsett promotes growing your own food, and Alex Robinson points to reducing waste

Your editorial is right to warn that Britain’s food system leaves us dangerously exposed (The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case, 15 October). But scarcity is only part of the problem. Across the country, good food exists; what is missing is the infrastructure to store it, aggregate it and get it to the people who need it.

That failure runs through the whole food chain. Farmers are being pushed to the brink while millions of tonnes of edible produce go to waste. Independent retailers and whol
title: Three ways to boost the UK’s fragile food security | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Phil Hamlyn Williams responds to criticism of the Church of England’s plans for reparations

Thank you for the excellent research into the rightwing backlash against the Church of England’s proposals for reparations (Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund, 13 October). May I offer observations in two areas?

We are all beneficiaries of the slave trade, like it or not. The work that the Guardian is doing on the actions of its founders will enhance the historical record, but it is unlikely to change the broader picture identified by Eric Hobsbawm and others.

Continue reading...
title: Like it or not, we have all benefited from the slave trade | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Elaine Hoare recalls her mother buying five fish for a shilling, while Michael Heaton draws readers’ attention to an Americanism

Your article (Whale meat curry for dinner? Study of bygone seafood recipes shows how UK tastes have narrowed, 13 October) reminded me of the call of “Fresh herring, fresh herring” from the herring man wheeling his cart in the back lane by our house in Douglas, Isle of Man, in the 1950s. My mother went to him with a bowl and bought herring for tea – five for a shilling, if I remember correctly. They were delicious. We cleaned them, scored each side three or four times, dipped them in oatmeal and fried them. We have a fish man from Grimsby call every Monday, but he never has herring.
Elaine Hoare
Chalfont St Giles, Buckinghamshire

• I am perplexed
title: A hankering for fresh herring and the proper British name for ‘sea bass’ | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Andrew James Sillett of St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals do

Dr Coco Parkinson-Huggins (Letters, 13 October) is right to highlight the severe financial pressures facing England’s cathedrals and the threat that this poses to choral music. Yet the future of choral evensong depends not just on cathedrals. Across the country, there are parish churches that sustain choirs, train young organists and offer regular opportunities for children and adults to participate in this living tradition.

I am a churchwarden and singer at St Giles’ church in Oxford, where locally recruited choirs of boys, girls and teenagers sing choral evensong every Sunday. Alongside these choirs, around 40 organ students are currently learning through the church, and we are investing in a major new pipe organ to support
title: Parish churches need support to preserve the tradition of choral evensong | Letter

author: John Crace
description:
The Tory leader has glimpsed the future and it involves Labour putting every last UK citizen on benefits

  • UK politics live – latest updates

If you’re worried about next week’s budget, then now is your time to chill out. Because Kemi Badenoch has all the answers. The chancellor, John Healey, has been living rent free in the leader of the opposition’s head for the past few weeks. Lucky man. More than that, she has been perched on his shoulder while he sits at his desk in the Treasury and tries to make the sums add up.

And – SPOILER ALERT – Kemi has now read the whole speech that hasn’t yet been written and is in a position to give her budget reply more than a week ahead of time. Opposition by telepathy. Or wish fulfilment. If things don’t work out for her in her current job she could
title: Nige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budget

author: Robert Tait in Washington
description:
Much of Donald Trump’s unpopularity in polls stems from dissatisfaction over the economy and war on Iran

  • US politics live – latest updates

***

Continue reading...
title: From Iran to AI: the six key voter issues shaping the US midterm elections

author: Caroline Davies
description:
Duke of Sussex says ‘there’s enough drama in the world’ without continuing to have issues with family

The Duke of Sussex wants to repair his difficult relationship with his father and brother, he has said.

Speaking to GQ magazine in New York, Prince Harry said of his complicated relationship with William and King Charles that from a family perspective it was a “massively relatable issue for so many people”.

Continue reading...
title: Prince Harry says he wants to reconcile with Charles and William

author: Geoff Lemon
description:
• Magnificent 179 puts hosts in charge on day three

  • Nic Maddison dismissed for a duck before close


In the first Test in Durban, it was Australia’s lower order hanging in with one established batter that first frustrated, then demoralised South Africa. In the second, on the third day in Gqeberha, South Africa returned the favour. Temba Bavuma played the role of Matthew Renshaw, assembling a near-flawless 179, combining with Marco Jansen’s 85 and Simon Harmer’s 82 to take the hosts to a declaration at 425 for 9. Australia then lost one wicket for three in reply.

Eight years ago, during Australia’s previous visit, Bavuma was a hard luck story. In his 29th Test and facing questioning for having only made one century in that time, he had Australia on the mat at Johannesburg in the aftermath of sandpaper week, until the last two wickets fell in two balls
title: Australia on the back foot as Bavuma plays captain’s innings for South Africa

author: Taha Hashim
description:
• England collapse after fast start to run chase

  • Arafat Minhas scores 59, then takes six for 40

After the embarrassment of their English summer this was a welcome sight for Pakistan. A contest in front of their own, no Ollie Robinson to wobble down a lethal Dukes ball, and a format they are far more comfortable with. The result was an impressive victory against England, who fell 87 runs short in their first match of this one-day international tri-series.

At the centre was Arafat Minhas, playing only his fifth ODI but already making a serious splash, finishing with astounding figures of six for 40. Oh, and he can bat too. The 21-year-old began with a half-century from No 7, resuscitating Pakistan’s innings alongside another newcomer, Hasan Nawaz, as 81 for four turned into a total of 302.

Continue reading...
title: Arafat rips through England as Brook’s men wilt against Pakistan in tri-series opener

author: Adria R Walker
description:
A new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaboration

In 1949, the poet and writer Langston Hughes was already a towering figure – he toured the country reading his poems and lecturing, drawing crowds that filled auditoriums. That year, at a lecture in Asheville, North Carolina, Hughes met a 16-year-old girl, Eunice Waymon, who would go on to make history in her own right using her stage name, Nina Simone.

Hughes and Simone became friends and collaborators, working together on songs such as Backlash Blues, which soundtracked what was then a nascent Black Power movement. The song influenced Kwame Ture, the activist and Black revolutionary who was then known as Stokely Carmichael, who popularized the phrase “Black power”.

Continue reading...
title: The little-known friendship between Nina Simone and Langston Hughes

author: David Hytner in Munich
description:
• Kompany told to rest after struggling with infection

  • His assistant poised to oversee Champions League game

Vincent Kompany is touch and go to be in the Bayern Munich dugout against Arsenal at the Allianz Arena on Wednesday night as he battles a debilitating virus that has affected his legs. Kompany was unable to attend his team’s training session on Tuesday before the Champions League tie, ceding the responsibility for the pre-match press conference to his assistant, Aaron Danks.

Kompany has been told to rest after he struggled through Bayern’s 6-1 home win over RB Leipzig in the Bundesliga on Saturday, after which the club’s sporting director, Max Eberl, addressed the media instead of him. There have been reports in Germany that Kompany needed to lie down on his sofa at home after the Leipzig game and that the viral infection had affected an existing hip problem which meant he could hardly walk.
title: Vincent Kompany to miss Bayern’s clash with Arsenal due to legs-affecting virus

author: Alan Evans
description:
A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse

• Don’t get Cluesletter, our weekly puzzles newsletter, delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

When the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, it was an early victory for artificial intelligence over the human mind, and the culmination of decades of attempts. Almost 30 years later, a computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords.

Earlier this month, a model called Darmok solved the final puzzle of the Times’s annual cryptic crossword competition about three minutes faster than Liam Hughes, 29, who became the contest’s youngest (human) winner.
title: Could this be a Deep Blue moment for the cryptic crossword?

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Click here to submit a picture for publication in these online galleries and/or on the Guardian letters page

Continue reading...
title: Nordic wonder and an ancient art – readers’ best photographs

author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
description:
City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building

Liverpool is to unveil a new 100,000 sq ft visitor attraction about the Beatles, in plans hailed as “extraordinary” by Paul McCartney, and by Andy Burnham as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain”.

Opening in 2028, the project is a huge upgrade for the Beatles Story, a museum which opened in Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock in 1990. Ownership will now pass to the Beatles company Apple Corps, making the Beatles Story the band’s first official fan experience in their home city.

Continue reading...
title: Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028

author: Helena Horton
description:
About 20,000 cats were taken into charity’s care last year, an increase driven in part by pet hoarders

There is a cat crisis in rescue centres across the country, the RSPCA has warned, as abandoned felines now outnumber dogs in the charity’s shelters.

Cats are arriving in RSPCA centres faster than they can be rehomed, and the charity is asking people across England and Wales to consider adopting. Pet owners are being urged to neuter their cats as kittens are increasingly being found dumped in perilous conditions.

Continue reading...
title: ‘We really need help’: RSPCA faces capacity crisis as cats arrive faster than they can be rehomed

author: Arwa Mahdawi
description:
The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power

What do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin? The president has claimed he has a problem with the progressive Democratic congresswoman because she is “unpatriotic” to the US and “disrespectful … to Israel”. However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it. Trump has insisted he is “the least racist person there is anywhere in the world”, so I’m sure it has nothing to do with the fact that she’s brown and Muslim. Truly, it’s a mystery.

W
title: Trump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new level | Arwa Mahdawi

author: George Francis Lee
description:
Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy

When Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.”

Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasingly enshittified.”
title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV

author: John Brewin
description:
As Tottenham edged to victory over Coventry, a familiar face among the post-match salutations. Could that be Dejan Kulusevski? For it was he, playing 526 days since his last Spurs appearance. Much has changed though still much stays the same. Ben Davies’s deflected late clincher catapulted Spurs up to … 16th. When Kulusevski last played on 11 May 2025, Tottenham were 17th, the position in which they finished both that season and in 2025-26.

Further to Peters and Lee [Monday’s Football Daily letters] another 70s example that occurred to me was the West Ham players Mervyn Day and Bill Green. They were both in the West Ham United team from 1976-78, and in Carlisle United’s greatest season 1974-75
title: Football Daily | Kulusevski and Maddison return to form but are Tottenham also back?

author: Blake Montgomery
description:
As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives

  • This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here

Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City. Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music, and a Guardian AI conference in Paris.
title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world

author: Andre Gee
description:
The Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at risk

Jalen Hurts is likely to miss the rest of the season after an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. Thankfully, he’s now restricted from playing for the immediate future, meaning he won’t be risking serious complications – or even his life – as he did when he played in their Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.

Hurts complained to the Eagles medical staff of calf pain on 8 October, according to ESPN. The Eagles say that Hurts flew to London with the rest of the team and, out of an “a
title: Jalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle?

author: Stuart Heritage
description:
As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show

When the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.

“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.
title: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and a caveman spinoff

author: Hannah Rochell
description:
Whether it’s Pfas-free tote bags or wash-in waterproofing, here’s how women can stay dry in style – and with less waste

• The best umbrellas – tested

After the hottest UK summer on record, autumn 2026 could be wetter and stormier than usual, partly because of the El Niño climate phenomenon, which is predicted to be the strongest of its kind in living memory. But a lot of wet-weather gear – from flimsy umbrellas that blow inside out within seconds to single-use ponchos that will sit in landfill long after this winter has blown over – often isn’t very sustainable.

While waterproofed polyester can keep us dry, there’s no excuse for it not to be made from recycled materials. Look instead for products that are designed to last and, better still, part of a circular system where the brand offers repairs and takes responsibility for reusing or recycling worn-out items
title: From granny hoods to recycled macs: 13 more sustainable ways to stay dry when it rains

author: Tim Byrne
description:
Starring a smooth-sprinting Tom Cruise at the top of his game, Steven Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller shows the scales falling from his own country’s eyes

I know, I know. There have been so many adaptations of HG Wells’ classic 1898 science fiction novel of planetary invasion, both before and since Steven Spielberg took his swipe at the story in 2005, with a Tom Cruise still at the top of his box office game. Some versions of War of the Worlds have been dire, while others – the 2019 TV adaptation starring Gabriel Byrne, or Jeff Wayne’s 1978 concept album featuring Richard Burton – have been expertly realised, refracting the story through their own contemporary lenses. But Spielberg’s is the best.

While it was a financial hit, Spielberg’s version was not universally loved. Peter Bradshaw, in his review for this masthead, called it “fundamentally unambitious and often quite dull”. So there! One of his strongest gripes was the design of the aliens themselves, which were “just
title: Spielberg’s War of the Worlds forced Americans to look in the mirror – and see the real monster

author: Shaad D'Souza
description:
Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back

Kiran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really, really hard not to swear.”

A decade ago, he explains, he was interviewed by the Guardian, got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. When the piece came out, his grandfather was thrilled. “But he couldn’t show any of his friends because I just sounded really aggressive,” he tells me sheepishly.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy

Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data to (China)’, defense department says

The US government on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from Chinese startup DeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.

A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed by DeepSeek – and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.

Female players including Carlinha and Tayla Carolina have spoken out against the far-right, who they fear will harm the women’s game as well as wider society

The day before the first round of Brazilian elections, the Estádio do Morumbi hosted the second leg of the Brazilian Women’s Championship final, in which São Paulo drew 1-1 with Corinthians to win 3-2 on aggregate and secure the Brasileirão Women’s title.

It had been an incredible final but after the game the goalkeeper Carlinha used an interview to appeal to her fans: “Never again Bolsonaro in power,” she shouted to a record-breaking TV audience of 23 million people.

UK government failures caused the Covid virus to spread “like wildfire” among vulnerable and elderly people, an inquiry has found. We’d like to hear your thoughts

Heather Hallett, who is leading the Covid-19 inquiry, said the care sector was “an afterthought” during the Covid-19 pandemic and it was a “significant omission” that the government did not advise that patients discharged from hospitals into care homes should be isolated, causing the virus to spread rapidly among residents and staff.

She also said preventing visits to care homes led to “immense emotional harm” for residents and left them with “profound isolation and a sense of abandonment”.

description:

A leading animal rights group has urged Crystal Palace to retire their American bald eagle mascot because, it says, the matchday experience can leave the bird “frightened, disoriented and panicked” and put spectators at risk.

In a letter to Palace’s chief executive, Sharon Lacey, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (Peta) called on the club to end Phoenix’s appearances at Selhurst Park and commit never to use a live animal mascot again.

author: Mark Lawson
description:
St John the Divine church, London
The poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relish

A striking example of site-specific theatre, TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral was first performed in 1935 at Canterbury Cathedral. This was the location, in 1170, for its pivotal event: the killing by Henry II’s knights of Archbishop Thomas Becket during a dispute over the powers of church and state.

Subsequently, audiences have been more likely to enter a production via a church nave than a theatre aisle. The latest host venue is St John the Divine, opposite the Orange Tree theatre, whose boss, Tom Littler, co-directs with Francesca Ellis.

Continue reading...
title: TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral review – gather in wonder at David Suchet’s excellent archbishop

description:
Yellow severe weather warning issued for first named storm of season with gusts of up to 60mph expected

The first named storm of the season, Austen, is expected to bring gusts of up to 60mph to southern areas of the UK at the end of the week, forecasters said.

While there would be spells of rain and showers for many on Tuesday and Wednesday, by Thursday Storm Austen would be approaching the south-west of the UK, the Met Office said.

title: Storm Austen forecast to hit southern UK

author: Catherine Shoard
description:
The actor’s forthcoming memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? says the makers had honourable intentions but the elements ‘didn’t coalesce’

Dame Judi Dench has long made her feelings clear about Cats, the doomed 2019 adaptation of the Andrew Lloyd Webber musical. In an interview the year after release, she said she had so far declined to watch the movie – in which she played wise moggy Old Deuteronomy – and described the orange fur coat she had to wear as looking like “five foxes fucking on my back”.

In her forthcoming memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? Dench reflects further on her involvement in the movie, which was universally panned and whose director, Tom Hooper, has not made a film since.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’

author: Rachel Aroesti
description:
A few months ago, he was pulling pints. How did he end up writing for Sharon Horgan, acting with Jeff Goldblum and storming the West End?

Until a few weeks ago, Freddie Meredith’s IMDb page was full of names like “Seb” and “George” and “Philip Noonan”. Lately, however, it’s started saying things like “Olly Murs” and “Liam Gallagher”. The characters that aren’t listed are even weirder: perhaps you’ve come across his recent turn as an east London mosquito? Or Jeff Goldblum’s troubled nephew? How about the tech billionaire tasked with introducing King Charles to a new AI assistant who looks exactly like Diana, Princess of Wales?

It’s not just Meredith’s online CV that has had a radical overhaul. At the start of this summer, the 33-year-old was working in a bar, where he would sometimes get recognised by fans of Bafta-winning BBC sitcom Such Brave Girls, in which he played the protagonist’s ludicrously tenacious boyfriend. He mimics punters’ confusion at seeing a guy off th
title: ‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leagues

author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
description:
RAF Typhoon fighters will fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure, in extension of UK support for Riyadh

RAF Typhoon fighters are to protect Saudi Arabia from attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying defensive missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure, as western allies step up their intervention in the escalating conflict.

The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, after attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities.

Continue reading...
title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks

description:

  • Former manager claims club broke promises made to him

Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo “let the team down” during their time together at Manchester United. Ten Hag has also alleged that promises made by United’s owners went unfulfilled, leading to his sacking by the club in October 2024.

Ronaldo returned for a second spell at United in August 2021 and was already at the club when Ten Hag was appointed in April 2022 as Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s successor. title: Erik ten Hag accuses Cristiano Ronaldo of ‘letting down’ Manchester United

author: Flora Willson
description:
Sohmen Concert Hall, Schwarzman Centre, Oxford
Six performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaboration

As we found our seats, a druidic figure wearing a string of vapes as a necklace sat on stage swathed in white fabric and smoke, emitting close-miked mouth noises amid a rising chorus of percussive hisses and rattles. Then dancing flashlights, reverb and thunderous drum rolls. Later came monologues delivered with quiet, skin-crawling sincerity or pounded out as a kind of manic rap and comically dysfunctional text chats projected on the backcloth. Not to mention the dance breaks. There was an angular, hyper-controlled trio fluent in the language of modern ballet and a hands-on-hips traditional number as faux-folk lyrics scrolled in gothic script and a hefty synthetic beat throbbed below.

The first collaboration between
title: The Alonetimes review – frenetic, funny and exhilarating music theatre

author: Felipe Maia
description:
Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission

Earlier this month, Brazil’s president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva led a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms.

More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups for Billie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, wa
title: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?

Young people in France, India and Albania and other parts of the world are protesting and we want to hear from them about the reasons why they’re taking to the streets

Young people in different parts of the world are protesting and we want to hear from them about the reasons they’re taking to the streets and on social media.

Across France there have been student-led rallies demanding action against inequality and staff shortages in schools. author: Sarah Rendell
description:
A first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten run

England’s glittering unbeaten era is over. Canada defeated the Red Roses to deal them a first defeat in four years after 40 wins and one draw. It was a landmark result for the Canadians, who will look to replicate the outcome this weekend when the two nations meet again. England must reset but they won’t panic; the Red Roses have been the standard bearers for the past seven years, which is why they have lost only twice in 73 matches. But while no team would ever aim to lose, falling to defeat is a good thing for England and the wider sport.

Losing could actually make England a deadlier team to face. That is because they now need to find another level to their game with teams beginning to figure out ways to beat them. They have been push
title: The Breakdown | ‘Freer’ Red Roses resolve to come back stronger after Canada end epic run

author: Kenneth Roth
description:
Here’s what we need to do to stand up for international law

Many applauded when Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel peace prize. The South African human rights lawyer had chaired the UN commission of inquiry that found Israel to have committed genocide in Gaza and served for five years as a judge on the international criminal court (ICC).

Donald Trump responded a few hours later by imposing sanctions on the ICC. He chose a moment for celebrating the rule of law to try to undermine it.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale Unive
title: We can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal court | Kenneth Roth

author: Cath Clarke
description:
With catches down 80%, dead crabs and lobsters washed up on beaches and officials denying any responsibility, Hartlepool seafarers have taken a stand

Hartlepool fisherman Stan Rennie has been called the next Mr Bates. For nearly 50 years Rennie has fished the same stretch of northeast coastline – then in October 2021, thousands of crabs, starfish and lobsters washed up dead and dying on the beaches. “It was like something out of a horror film,” says one local. Rennie and other fishermen suspected industrial pollution, but an investigation by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs concluded that the most likely cause of the die-off was “algal bloom”. For Rennie and the other fisherman, it didn’t add up. So, they crowdfunded their own independent scientific study.

This documentary from Jeani
title: All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activism

author: Zoe Williams
description:
I’m never fully concentrating, always simultaneously thinking a huge thought about the future or scrolling through Vinted

Some friends and I were talking, at the weekend, about the TV shows War (about a couple getting divorced) and The Diplomat (about an entirely different couple, not getting divorced). I hadn’t seen either because I was busy with Colin from Accounts. One friend had seen one show but not the other, and couldn’t remember which; a second friend had seen both and couldn’t remember anything that happened in either.

It emphatically wasn’t because they weren’t good. The second friend seemed medium-sure, in fact, that they were both great. His thesis is that he just watches so much TV that none of it can find any purchase in his memory.

Continue reading...
title: That piping hot new TV show I just watched? I can’t recall a thing about it | Zoe Williams

author: Carlos Mureithi in Obock
description:
Their overland routes to safety blocked off, several thousand people have boarded boats to escape gunfire, bombing and a dire humanitarian situation

Abubaker Saeed was fishing in the Red Sea off Yemen’s coast last month when he noticed explosions in the distance. His mind turned immediately to his wife and two children, and he raced back to his home village of al-Wahijah.

Aircraft from the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemeni government forces had launched airstrikes in surrounding areas, targeting members of the Iran-aligned Houthi militia as its fighters approached the nearby port city of Mocha.

Continue reading...
title: Fleeing the frontline: Yemeni families cross Red Sea to Djibouti as Houthi conflict rages

author: Jessica Rawnsley in Panama
description:
Failed rains and a dire El Niño threaten the waterway that sustains the country, with farmers selling cattle to survive

The cattle should be ambling, grazing contentedly, through Robert Delgado’s fields. Instead, the animals slump in the shade, tongues lolling, in futile attempts to avoid the blistering heat. Soon it will matter little whether their appetite returns, for there will be no grass left to graze.

In Azuero, an agricultural region in Panama’s Arco Seco (Dry Arc), the summer is generally relentless and unforgiving. But this year, the crucial rainy season that precedes it – typically from May to December – has brought little rain to parched fields. The watering holes, streams and rivers that farmers rely on have not been replenished, and pastures – the vital source of animal feed during the dry months – have not regenerated themselves.
title: ‘For Panama, it is life or death’: how drought is choking the canal that feeds a nation

author: Paul Taylor
description:
The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher

There is only one clear winner so far from France’s chaos: Marine Le Pen.

The violence and rioting that engulfed towns and cities across the country over the weekend, six months before a pivotal presidential election, is a godsend for the hard-right, Eurosceptical, anti-immigration candidate. As buildings burned, shops were looted and police attacked, the rioting largely drowned out peaceful mass protests over the dilapidated state of schools , fuel prices and the cost of living.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre
title: After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul Taylor

Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday

Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupeesvaluation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.

author: Imogen West-Knights
description:
I have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with these dramas told in episodes under two minutes, I swear I can actually feel the damage being done

Seven or eight years ago, a new kind of televisual entertainment was born in China. Microdramas: over-the-top, soap opera-type series with splashy, schlocky premises such as infidelity, arranged marriage and secret billionairehood, in which each episode is a mere 60-90 seconds long, took off there among an audience of the phone-addicted.

And now, as with many cultural phenomena that start in China, microdramas have made it over here. The form is forecast to take in $1.5bn in revenue in the US by the end of this year. Channel 4 announced recently that it was
title: I thought my phone couldn’t be any worse for my brain – then I started watching microdramas on it | Imogen West-Knights

author: Sam Wollaston
description:
These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?

Who knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at the Monaco Yacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?

To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.
title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show

author: Martin Pengelly
description:
The Pulitzer prize-winning writer’s new book looks at the women on death row in Texas and the nuns who have been trying to help them

It is “stunning”, the Pulitzer-winning reporter Lawrence Wright said, that Redemption, his new book about women on death row in Texas and the nuns who minister to them, turns out to be published at a time of intense focus on capital punishment.

Two cases dominate headlines: the Trump administration’s abandoned plan to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, and Tennessee’s failure to kill the convicted murderer Christa Pike by lethal injection. Away from the headlines, in Texas and elsewhere, exe
title: ‘It speaks very poorly of us as a society’: Lawrence Wright on his book on death row and redemption

description:
Our writers give their verdicts on the new season, which tips off Tuesday. Who will claim the title? And which youngster will make the superstar leap?

Seeing all the fruits borne of an incredible summer of player movement. It feels like three years ago that Giannis Antetokounmpo was traded to the Heat, because since then, Jaylen Brown and LeBron James went to the 76ers, and a ton of other deck chairs were reshuffled. This is the most intriguing NBA opening week in eons. Claire de Lune

author: Gynelle Leon
description:
Cutting out dead material will make the plant look better without damaging it. But be careful not to slice into the living leaf

The problem
You can really love your plants and still be rewarded with crispy, brown leaf tips. While they won’t kill your plant, they aren’t aesthetically pleasing.

The hack
The tidy-up is simple: cut off the dry, brown parts of the leaf. The plant looks instantly better, and the theory is this does no harm because the tissue is already dead. But the worry is it will hurt the plant or make the browning worse.

Continue reading...
title: Houseplant hacks: will trimming brown leaf tips do any harm?

author: Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent
description:
With living memory fading and thousands of Welsh coal tips still posing a threat, a community robbed of justice reflects on how to keep legacy alive

David Davies was eight years old when he survived the coal tip slide that killed a generation of children in the Welsh village of Aberfan. Most years the disaster’s anniversary passes quietly, he says; much of the community chooses to spend the day reflecting and mourning in the privacy of their homes.

His own recollection of what happened on the cloudy autumn morning in 1966 is hazy. His father, one of the volunteers who uncovered the corpses of more than 100 children from the buried Pantglas primary school, said that when he was handed his son’s unconscious body, he initially thought he was dead.

Continue reading...
title: ‘I survived for a reason’: Aberfan fights to preserve memory of disaster 60 years on

author: Tom Burgis
description:
Apparent attempt to hack Rade Bajić’s iPhone comes amid efforts to undermine landmark criminal case

A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates.

The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities.

Continue reading...
title: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
Exclusive: Adrian Ramsay calls conference motion a distraction and says councillors should maintain coalitions where possible

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader of the Greens, has urged his party’s councillors to reject the newly adopted “Zionism is racism” motion if it will help them stay in power in local government, in a fresh sign of internal dissent over the policy.

Ramsay, one of the Greens’ five MPs, said he was pleased that a number of Green council groups had already condemned the policy, which was adopted at the party’s conference and also calls for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.
title: Ex-Greens co-leader urges council groups to reject Zionism policy

author: Chloë Ashby
description:
This collection of essays from the beloved novelist is full of gem-like insights on art and books

When Tessa Hadley was a child, someone gave her a copy of Lois Lenski’s Papa Small, which follows Mr Small and his family through a typical week. Papa Small goes to work, Mama Small cooks the supper, and the small Smalls dry and put away the dishes. “I thrilled to its ordinariness,” writes Hadley, a novelist known for her depictions of the ordinary that are anything but. In all her novels and short stories, she’s spectacularly alive to the everyday, both the seemingly humdrum surfaces and the darkest emotional depths.

So you know what you’re in for when you reach for a book by Hadley, which is why I was in equal parts excited and apprehensive about her first foray into nonfiction. At least, it’s her first in bound form: Alone With a Book comprises published essays written since 2000. A nimble mix of biography, cultural criticism and person
title: Alone With a Book by Tessa Hadley review – an acclaimed writer’s cultural prescription

author: Geoff Lemon (now) and Daniel Gallan (later)
description:

Mulder follows suit.

author: Nils Pratley
description:
As long as Healey doesn’t go overboard, a small turn on surcharge dial will not seriously undermine flow of capital

Everyone is familiar with the banks’ plea: raising taxes on them amounts to taxing the nation’s growth. If you increase how much banks pay, goes the argument, less interest will be paid on deposits and loans will cost slightly more, meaning we’ll all be worse off eventually. In terms of economic theory, it’s coherent, it should be said: in an ideal world, a chancellor would strive to lower costs of capital at every opportunity.

In the real world, however, John Healey faces multiple competing demands, even from within a business lobby that extends well beyond the banks. As this newspaper revealed last week, the chancellor is likely to increase bank taxes in his budget next week. In the current climate of trying to
title: A modest increase in bank taxes is not the end of the world for lenders | Nils Pratley

author: Catherine Bray
description:
A scrappy girl discovers her tribe – which includes a vegan vampire – at a school for top scarers in this entertaining pre-teen animation

In films, twins are usually written as either identical personalities or complete and total opposites, and it’s the latter dynamic that’s at work in this pre-teen animation. One twin is a popular straight-A student heavily invested in fitting in and doing well at ballet, while her sister Mia is a chaotic kook. They both live in Primrose, an appropriately named community that apparently used to be infested with monsters, but can now claim to be proudly monster-free for the last 500 years. The twins’ parents are supportive of their golden child and try their best to understand Mia too, but it is easier for them to praise the kid bringing home the perfect behaviour reports than the one exasperating her teachers with her determination to discover monsters, by hook or by crook.

Scrappy Mia is, naturally, the protagonist of this film
title: Monster Mia review – kooky kid discovers school of beastly besties in wholesome Halloween fun

author: Chris Wiegand Stage editor
description:
Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos Morau

‘Let’s dance,” sang David Bowie in 1983, commanding: “Put on your red shoes and dance the blues.” That call is to be answered – with footwear TBC – by an international dance production featuring new choral arrangements of songs from throughout his career.

Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will be staged at Sadler’s Wells in London in autumn 2028 after a world premiere in Luxembourg. It will visit Tokyo in 2029. The show will explore how Bowie “practised a form of artistic reincarnation” according to Spanish choreographer Marcos Morau who is taking inspiration from the superstar’s transformations into personas such as Aladdin Sane and the Thin White Duke.

Continue reading...</
title: Getting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songs

author: Joe Todd
description:
The party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement it

It’s a strange time to be a Green. We have just held our largest conference ever, but it was overshadowed by a controversial motion that was attacked by the media as racist. Then, when we lost a byelection in a Camden seat that is so Labour it has estates named after Blair-era ministers, the headlines called for Zack Polanski to resign.

It does, however, mark the end of phase one for Polanski’s Greens. Polanski burst on to the political scene in 2025 and ate up attention, enjoying an easy monopoly on hope while Labour was sucked into the black hole of Starmerism. Labour has since escaped, with Andy Burnham giving social democracy with Mancunian characteristics a half-hearted go. But Burnham’s honeymoon already seems to be e
title: What’s the future for the Green Party? Should it be socialism? | Joe Todd

author: Graeme Wearden
description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

The government should not be complacent about the state of the labour market ahead of next week’s budget, warns Ben Harrison, director of the Work Foundation at Lancaster University:

Harrison explains:

The UK is still amidst a jobs drought with vacancies at their lowest for over 12 years outside of the pandemic.

“In particular, there are now 715,000 young people aged 16–24 unemployed, down by 28,000 on the quarter. Nevertheless, the number of young people out of work remains 54,000 higher than 12 months ago.

“While the labour market remains broadly flat in 2026, data from the latest quarter shows the employment rate edging up and a small drop in unemployment. The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that
title: UK unemployment rate falls in pre-budget boost, but firms keep cutting vacancies – business live

author: Niha Masih
description:
​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.

That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.

Continue reading...
title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home

author: Rhiannon Batten
description:
The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages

Bracken and heather ripple across the plateau. I exhale into the chill autumn air and my breath mists a view that reaches all the way to Gower and the ochre peaks of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly the Brecon Beacons). Far below, the Ogmore valley’s terrace houses look like tiny constellations but up here on Tarren y Fforch, it’s just me and a few sheep taking springy steps between tufts of bilberries. If this corner of the south Wales valleys feels a long way from its coal mining past, that is, partly, the point.

I’m hiking the new Llwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail, or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what the
title: ‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trail

author: Sarah Marsh, Consumer affairs correspondent
description:
Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong

After Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed the parcel arrived empty.

Warrilow, 47, from Oxford, provided Vinted with photos and videos of the package, including date-stamped Ring doorbell footage of her leaving the house to post it. But she says the resale platform refunded the buyer and left her out of pocket.

Continue reading...
title: ‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’

author: Leslie Felperin
description:
Tense story fritters away initial levels interest as generic horrors eclipse offbeat family dynamic

This gloomy-toned film takes its sweet time revealing its genre nature, emerging as a proper horror flick more than halfway in with a detailed transformation sequence. It’s the sort of showreel stuff that special effects technicians and aficionados revel in, although others might find the creature design a little plasticky, not unlike the things we see being 3D-printed elsewhere in the feature.

It’s a shame that the hardcore creature-feature stuff is a letdown because the drama leading up to it isn’t bad. We start with a forensic science expert called Meg (Deborah Ann Woll), a young woman whose shiny hair and perky professional attitude disguises a steely composure and strong stomach that’s not in the slightest bit discombobulated by all the rotting, decomposing flesh she deals with on the daily.
title: The Cycle review – forensic scientist autopsies her dad in grisly psychodrama that turns supernatural

author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
description:
Around one in eight 16- to 24-year-olds are ‘Neet’ – and Alan Milburn is hinting that the overhaul of their support may be controversial

With nearly 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (a cohort known as “Neets”), the government and its advisers have signalled that welfare benefits may be cut to fund more job support for them. What may change and who will be affected?

Continue reading...
title: Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?

author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
description:
Projection delivers a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected.

With more than one million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation.

Continue reading...
title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada, CBC projects

author: Hollie Richardson, Jack Seale, Ali Catterall and Ellen E Jones
description:
In an eye-opening documentary, she meets long-term ketamine users. Plus: never-before-seen clips from Only Fools and Horses. Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC Three
To be clear, Stacey Dooley says she has never taken ketamine. But it is one of the most popular recreational drugs among those under 24, so she is meeting some of the long-term users who are living with the consequences. From learning about “ket bladder” (passing blood or parts of an eroding bladder in the urine) to hearing how much the drug helps them to “dissociate”, the conversations are eye-opening and often heartbreaking. Hollie Richardson

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: Stacey Dooley learns about ‘ket bladder’

author: Presented by Matilda Boseley with Tom McIlroy; produced by Cheyne Anderson; sound design and mixing by Daniel Semo; video production Rachel Herron; executive producer is Hannah Parkes
description:
Helen Haines, the independent federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, is in a critical condition and has lost a leg after an alleged attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon.

On Tuesday the alleged attacker and driver of the car was named by police as 43-year-old Brendan Nugent.

A major investigation is under way into the incident, with Victoria police, the Australian federal police, Asio and counter-terrorism investigators involved.

Guardian Australian political editor Tom McIlroy speaks to Matilda Boseley about what happened and why this alleged attack on an independent MP is a watershed moment in Australian politics and political debate

Read more:

Helen Haines loses leg after car allegedly did U-turn and struck her twice in Wangaratta
title: What the Helen Haines tragedy means for Australian democracy – podcast

author: Gaby Hinsliff
description:
The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost

Another morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.

In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to
title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite | Gaby Hinsliff

author: Sami Tamimi
description:
Serve this warm and juicy meatball sabanekh with Iraqi tomato rice for a comforting meal that’s made to be shared

This is the kind of meal I love for its generosity and simplicity. A comforting spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh), scattered with tender lamb meatballs and finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. And, alongside, Iraqi red rice (timman ahmar) brings warmth, colour and a gentle sweetness from the tomato, and soaks up the rich, savoury juices of the stew. Together, they form a hearty meal made for sharing.

Continue reading...
title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red rice

author: Mark Cocker
description:
Ouse Fen, Cambridgeshire: The great egret’s story is remarkable, as is the conversion of this low-grade agricultural land into one of the richest wetlands in Britain

In keeping with this region’s summer of torrid heat and drought, the field by the path was an expanse of burnt, dead thistles. What was totally unexpected were the 13 great egrets among it. Ironically, the birds may well be here as a consequence of the climate crisis, but their appearance in a parched brown expanse felt strange.

First, they are creatures of freshwater marsh and routinely hunt fish. Second, great egrets are the size of grey herons, but pure white, aside from lemon eyes and dagger-like beaks of pale autumnal orange. What was weirdest of all was the gestalt whole; the way they threaded through that horizon of brown, long necks extending
title: Country diary: A species brought to the edge of extinction, recovering in the fens | Mark Cocker

author: Kate Wyver
description:
Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptation

The woodland is stuck to our skin. Sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price are hunched next to me, burying a microphone into mossy ground. Composer Dom Coyote is listening on headphones, crunching out a rhythm with his boot before shucking his shoes for a subtler sound. “It’s got to be socks off, Dom,” says Price. Coyote obliges, the balls of his feet soon covered in dead conifer needles. “Do you wish you’d had a pedicure now?” Peña asks.

It’s a short drive from Bristol to this patch on the Mendip Hills, where pine cones and rowan berries scatter at the entrance to the trees. We’re on the hunt for sounds to orchestrate a staging of Max Porter’s novel Lanny. The adaptation by Somerset-based Bea Roberts
title: Listen for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale be heard in this woodland?

author: Agencies
description:
• Tampa Bay beat Guardians to seal ALCS in six games

  • 7-3 Game 6 win set up by strong Freddy Peralta start

Freddy Peralta threw 5.1 gritty innings, Junior Caminero and Yandy Díaz each hit a two-run homer and the Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Monday night to advance to the World Series for the third time in the franchise’s 29 seasons.

The Rays will face the Milwaukee Brewers who, like Tampa Bay, are seeking to win their first-ever World Series. A sellout crowd of 40,230 fans waved yellow-and-blue rally towels, rang cowbells and chanted “Let’s go Rays!” throughout the night at Tropicana Field, which needed major renovations after Hurricane Milton shredded the roof two years ago and caused extensive damage throughout the stadium.

Continue reading...
title: World Series will have first-time champion as Rays set up showdown with Brewers

author: Guardian staff and agencies
description:
Ukrainian president tells US senators the delayed missiles have already been paid for by European countries, amid growing rift. What we know on day 1,700

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US is deliberately delaying deliveries of interceptor missiles to Ukraine, deepening a public spat with Donald Trump. Speaking to US senators on Monday, the Ukrainian president claimed that “the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles” already paid for by European countries under the prioritised Ukraine requirements list (Purl) program. According to Zelenskyy, the shipment is awaiting the signature of the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. A White House official, who spoke to the Washington Post on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy, said the US “continues to play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working
title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv
